title: Poor Pigs
statement:
Exactly one of `buckets` buckets of liquid is poisoned, and you identify it by feeding pigs. You have `minutesToTest` minutes in total, used in rounds:

- At the start of a round, pick any of the pigs that are still alive and, for each one, any set of buckets. A pig drinks all of its chosen buckets instantly; one pig may drink from many buckets and one bucket may be given to many pigs.
- Then wait `minutesToDie` minutes without feeding anything. At the end of the wait, every pig that drank from the poisoned bucket dies and every other pig stays alive.
- Start another round if enough time remains for a full wait.

Return the smallest number of pigs that guarantees you can tell which bucket is poisoned before the time runs out.
signature: int poorPigs(int buckets, int minutesToDie, int minutesToTest)
notes:
## Intuition

Only the number of rounds matters: `T = floor(minutesToTest / minutesToDie)`. Watch a single pig over the whole test: it dies after round 1, after round 2, ..., after round `T`, or it survives. That is `T + 1` possible outcomes. With `p` pigs the combined outcome is one of `(T + 1)^p` patterns, so no strategy can separate more buckets than that.

It is also enough. Number the buckets in base `T + 1` with one digit per pig. If a bucket's digit for pig `j` is `d < T`, pig `j` drinks it in round `d + 1`; if the digit is `T`, pig `j` never drinks it. The rounds in which the pigs die (or that they survive) spell out the poisoned bucket's number. So the answer is the smallest `p` with `(T + 1)^p >= buckets`.

## Approach

1. Compute `states = floor(minutesToTest / minutesToDie) + 1`, the outcomes one pig can show.
2. Start with `pigs = 0` and `reach = 1` (with no pigs, one bucket is already identified).
3. While `reach < buckets`, add a pig: multiply `reach` by `states` and increase `pigs`.
4. Return `pigs`.

## Example 1, step by step

`buckets = 4`, `minutesToDie = 15`, `minutesToTest = 15`: one round, so `states = 2`. `reach` goes `1 → 2` (`pigs = 1`) and `2 → 4` (`pigs = 2`). Now `reach = 4` is not below `4`, so the answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log buckets): `reach` at least doubles each step.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- The number of rounds uses floor division: `29` minutes with `minutesToDie = 15` allow only one round.
- A pig has `T + 1` outcomes, not `T`: surviving the whole test is information too.
- `Math.ceil(Math.log(buckets) / Math.log(states))` can be off by one: `Math.log(125) / Math.log(5)` is `3.0000000000000004`. Integer multiplication avoids this.
- One bucket needs `0` pigs.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `states` | outcomes one pig can show: dies in one of the rounds or survives |
| `pigs` | pigs used so far |
| `reach` | buckets that `pigs` pigs can tell apart, `states^pigs` |

narration.2: Each pig can die after any of the rounds or survive them all, so it shows rounds + 1 different outcomes.
narration.4: With no pigs only one bucket can be told apart.
narration.5: Keep adding pigs while the outcome patterns cannot yet cover every bucket.
narration.6: Each new pig multiplies the number of distinguishable patterns by states.
narration.9: This is the fewest pigs whose patterns cover all buckets.
